title: Corporate Finance: How Businesses Decide
description: How a company decides which projects to fund, how to pay for them and how much to give back to its owners, with a learner judging each choice rather than computing it.
audience: A capable adult who can read a balance sheet and income statement and has met compound interest, expected value and diversification. They want to judge whether a project, a borrowing, a payout or an acquisition makes sense, using Australian companies and tax where the sources allow.
outcomes: You'll be able to compare a payment now with a payment later and say what rate makes them equal.
You'll be able to say whether a project creates value, which cash flows belong in the answer, and when IRR or payback gives the wrong one.
You'll be able to explain what a required return is made of, what debt and equity each cost, and why a project needs a rate that matches its own risk.
You'll be able to judge whether a firm should borrow more, pay out cash or buy back shares, and say what a franked dividend is worth to a given shareholder.
You'll be able to find the assumption an answer depends on and check a forecast against what happened to similar projects.
You'll be able to say whether an acquisition price can pay off and what a share price can and cannot tell a manager.

lessons.title: Money now and money later
lessons.objective: Compare a payment now with a larger payment later by asking what the money could earn elsewhere, and say which is worth more and at what rate the answer flips.

concepts.title: Time value of money
concepts.summary: Money in hand can be invested, so the same sum is worth more now than later.

concepts.title: Discount rate
concepts.summary: The return given up by waiting: what the same money would earn in the best alternative of the same risk.

concepts.title: Present value
concepts.summary: The value today of money due later, found by discounting it at the discount rate.

concepts.title: Break-even rate
concepts.summary: The rate at which waiting and not waiting are worth the same; below it waiting wins, above it taking the money now wins.

misconceptions: More dollars later always beats fewer dollars now. The extra has to be set against what the money could have earned meanwhile.
Money has a time value only because prices rise. Wikipedia's own example is £100 now against £105 in a year at 5% with zero inflation.
The right rate is what the firm pays on its own loan. It is what the money could earn in the best alternative of the same risk.
A higher discount rate makes a distant payment worth more. It makes it worth less, because waiting costs more.
sequence: Open on a choice a firm really faces: a customer offers to pay now or pay more later. Ask what the firm could do with the cash in between.
Name the idea: money in hand can be invested, so waiting has a price. Show that this holds at zero inflation.
Turn the price of waiting into a rate, and then into a present value: how much is the later payment worth today at that rate?
Find the break-even rate, and read the choice on each side of it. The same offer is good at 5% and poor at 10%.
Show that a bond price is exactly this calculation: the RBA's example of a bond whose price rises to $109.50 when the required yield falls from 2% to 1%.
Close on the two parts of a required return, payment for waiting and payment for risk, and say that the second part is the subject of lessons 6 to 8.
examples: Invented: a customer will pay $100,000 now or $108,000 in a year. The firm can earn 5% on safe money: the $108,000 is worth about $102,900 today, so wait. At 10% it is worth about $98,200, so take the cash. The two are equal at 8%.

Invented: $150,000 in five years against $100,000 now. At 6% the later sum is worth about $112,100; at 9% about $97,500; break-even is about 8.4%. A dollar due in ten years is worth about 46 cents at 8% and about 68 cents at 4%.
RBA: a $100 government bond paying $2 a year is worth $100 to investors who require 2%; if the required yield falls to 1% its price rises to $109.50.

lessons.title: Value that arrives late
lessons.objective: Judge how much of a long cash stream's value arrives in the early years and how much far out, and say which streams a change in the discount rate hurts most.

concepts.title: Annuity
concepts.summary: A series of equal payments at regular intervals.

concepts.title: Perpetuity
concepts.summary: Payments that continue forever; with a steady payment its value is the payment divided by the rate.

concepts.title: Terminal value
concepts.summary: The value placed on all cash flows after the years that are forecast in detail; often a large share of a valuation.

concepts.title: Rate sensitivity
concepts.summary: The further out a payment is, the more a change in the discount rate moves its present value.

misconceptions: A 30-year stream is worth about 30 times its first payment. Late payments are heavily discounted, but they still carry a large share.
A rise of a few points in the rate hurts every cash flow about equally. It hurts distant payments far more than near ones.
Terminal value is a small tail added at the end. In many valuations it is a large share, and it is very sensitive to the rate and growth assumptions.
A growing perpetuity can be valued with any growth rate. The formula only works when growth is below the discount rate.
sequence: Start from a table of $100 a year for 30 years and the present value of each payment at 6%. Ask where the value sits.
Compare the first ten years with the whole: about half the value at 6% and about two thirds at 10%.
Raise the rate from 6% to 10% and compare a 5-year stream with a 30-year stream. Name the idea: rate sensitivity.
Introduce the perpetuity and the terminal value as ways of valuing everything past the forecast. Show why growth must stay below the rate.
Read Woolworths' impairment note: a long-term growth rate of 2.5% and a one-point rise in the discount rate plus a 10% cut in terminal-year profit that removes the headroom in New Zealand Food.
Close on what to ask of any valuation: how much of it comes after year ten, and what happens if the rate is a point higher?
examples: Invented: $100 a year for 30 years. At 6% it is worth about $1,376, of which the first ten years carry about $736 (54%). At 10% it is worth about $943, and the first ten years carry about $614 (65%).
The same rise from 6% to 10% cuts a 30-year stream by about 31% and a 5-year stream by about 10%.
Invented: $100 a year forever is worth $1,000 at 10% and about $1,667 at 6%.

Woolworths, 2026: long-term growth rate 2.5%; post-tax discount rates from 8.6% (New Zealand Food) to 11.2% (Quantium); for New Zealand Food a 1.0 point rise in the rate with a 10% cut in terminal-year EBIT would bring the recoverable value down to its carrying value.

lessons.title: Net present value
lessons.objective: Decide whether a project creates value by comparing its cost with the present value of what it returns at the rate investors require, and read the answer as value added today.

concepts.title: Net present value
concepts.summary: The present value of a project's cash flows less its cost: the value it adds, in today's dollars, over what investors could earn elsewhere.

concepts.title: Required return (hurdle rate)
concepts.summary: The return investors could earn on other investments of the same risk; the discount rate in an NPV.

concepts.title: Independent projects
concepts.summary: Projects that can all be undertaken if each adds value and capital is not short; their NPVs add.

concepts.title: Zero NPV
concepts.summary: A project that earns exactly the required return: it neither adds nor loses value.

misconceptions: NPV is accounting profit. It is value created over the investors' alternative.
A project that gets its money back or shows a profit must be worth doing. It also has to beat what the money could earn elsewhere.
A negative NPV means the project loses money. It means the return is below the required return, which can still be positive.
A zero NPV means the project failed. It means the project earns exactly the required return.
sequence: Put three fit-outs side by side with the same cost and different cash flows, and ask which are worth doing before any number is computed.
Show the present value of each one's inflows against its cost, and name the difference NPV.
Read the three results: value added, break-even and value destroyed, and say what the break-even one earns.
Say what a negative NPV does not mean, and what a positive one means for independent projects.
Say what NPV leaves out or depends on: non-financial benefits, the forecasts, and the choice of rate. That leads to lessons 4, 8 and 12.
examples: Invented: three fit-outs each cost $1,000,000 and run for five years, discounted at 8%. A returns $300,000 a year: inflows are worth about $1,198,000 and NPV is about +$198,000. B returns $250,000: inflows about $998,000, NPV about zero. C returns $200,000: inflows about $799,000, NPV about -$201,000. C hands back its whole $1,000,000 and still destroys value.
NPVs add: A together with an independent project of NPV +$40,000 adds about $238,000.

questionPlan.answer: Self-rated. A good answer says the money comes back later than it was paid out, investors could have earned the required return on it in the meantime, and NPV counts that lost return.

lessons.title: Which cash flows count
lessons.objective: Sort the items in a project proposal into the cash flows that belong in its NPV and those that do not: sunk costs, opportunity costs, side effects, working capital, tax and financing costs.

concepts.title: Incremental cash flow
concepts.summary: Cash that changes because the project goes ahead, compared with the firm without it.

concepts.title: Sunk cost
concepts.summary: Money already spent or committed that cannot be recovered whatever is decided; it stays out.

concepts.title: Opportunity cost
concepts.summary: The best use of an owned asset that the project gives up; it counts even though no cash is paid out.

concepts.title: Side effect
concepts.summary: A change to the firm's other products or costs caused by the project, including lost sales of existing products.

concepts.title: Working capital as a cash flow
concepts.summary: Stock, receivables and cash floats tie up cash at the start and release it at the end.

misconceptions: Money already spent on the project must be recovered by it. Past spending is the same whether or not the project goes ahead, so it cannot affect the choice.
An asset the firm already owns is free to use. Its best alternative use or sale is given up.
Interest on the funding should be deducted from the project's cash flows. The cost of funding is already in the discount rate, so deducting it counts it twice.
All of a new product's sales are new sales. Some may be taken from the firm's existing products.
Profit and cash flow are the same. Stock and customer credit take cash that profit does not show.
sequence: Give one proposal with ten items and ask which of them change the firm's cash if it goes ahead.
Name the test: incremental cash flow, the firm with the project against the firm without it.
Take the items out in groups: sunk costs out; owned assets in at their opportunity cost; side effects in; financing out.
Add working capital and tax, and show them as cash flows at the start, during and at the end.
Show the sunk-cost mistake in real organisations: utility managers slow to stop unviable nuclear plants, and the Concorde.
Close on a checklist for any proposal.
examples: Invented: a roaster plans a café in a shop it owns and currently lets for $60,000 a year. Counted: the fit-out; the lost rent; the contribution lost on its wholesale beans; $25,000 of extra stock at the start, recovered at the end; tax on the extra profit; the café's extra profit. Left out: the $30,000 survey already paid; $15,000 a year of interest on the bank loan; dividends paid to owners.

Real pattern: Wikipedia reports (De Bondt and Makhija, 1988) that managers of many US utilities were slow to end unviable nuclear plant projects, and that the Concorde went on being funded after the economic case had gone.

lessons.title: IRR and payback: where they mislead
lessons.objective: Compare projects by NPV, IRR and payback, say which rule to trust when they disagree, and spot the cases where IRR or payback gives the wrong answer.

concepts.title: Internal rate of return
concepts.summary: The discount rate at which a project's NPV is zero: the return it earns.

concepts.title: Payback period
concepts.summary: The time taken for a project's cash flows to repay its cost; it ignores timing and what comes after.

concepts.title: Mutually exclusive projects
concepts.summary: Projects of which at most one can be undertaken, such as two designs for the same site.

concepts.title: Multiple IRRs
concepts.summary: A project whose cash flows change sign more than once can have more than one IRR, or none that make sense.

misconceptions: The project with the highest IRR is the best. With mutually exclusive projects a bigger project can have a lower IRR and a higher NPV.
A quick payback means a good project. Payback ignores what happens after it and ignores timing within it.
IRR is a single number for any project. A project that has an outflow at the end, such as a mine or a nuclear plant, can have several.
Payback is worthless. It is quick and fits similar small investments, and the sources say so.
Executives prefer IRR, so it must be right. Wikipedia reports that preference alongside an academic preference for NPV.
sequence: Define IRR as the rate at which NPV is zero, and show that for one ordinary project it agrees with NPV.
Put two mutually exclusive projects of different size side by side: the small one has the higher IRR, the large one the higher NPV.
Add a third rule, payback, and a project that pays back fast but destroys value.
Show the project that pays out late and large and loses on payback but wins on NPV.
Show a project with a clean-up cost at the end and its two IRRs, both above the hurdle, with a negative NPV.
Close with the rule of thumb: NPV first; IRR and payback as summaries, not as deciders.
examples: Invented, required return 8%: S costs $100 and returns $60 a year for 3 years (IRR 36%, NPV about +$55, payback 1.7 years); L costs $1,000 and returns $400 a year for 4 years (IRR 22%, NPV about +$325, payback 2.5 years). On one site only one can be built: IRR picks S, NPV picks L. L has the higher NPV at any rate below about 20.5%.

Invented: P costs $1,000 and returns $500 in each of two years: payback exactly 2 years, NPV about -$108. Q costs $1,000 and returns $200, $200, $300, $400, $600, $600: payback 3.75 years, NPV about +$675, IRR 23.6%.

lessons.title: Risk and required return
lessons.objective: Explain why riskier cash flows are discounted at higher rates, separate the risk investors are paid for from the risk they can remove by holding many shares, and rank businesses by how much they move with the economy.

concepts.title: Risk-free rate
concepts.summary: The return on an investment assumed to meet every payment, usually a government bond in the same currency; the base of every required return.

concepts.title: Risk premium
concepts.summary: The extra return investors demand for cash flows that may not arrive.

concepts.title: Systematic and firm-specific risk
concepts.summary: Systematic risk is common to all shares and cannot be diversified away; firm-specific risk can, so the market does not pay for it.

concepts.title: Beta
concepts.summary: How much a share tends to move with the market as a whole; the average share has a beta of 1.

misconceptions: All risk earns a higher return. Only the risk that cannot be diversified away is paid for.
A risk-free rate means no risk at all. Government bonds are free of default risk in their own currency, but still carry interest rate and inflation risk.
Beta is a measure of how risky a business is overall. It measures co-movement with the market, which is related to total risk but is not the same.
A high beta means a bad business. It means the cash flows move strongly with the economy.

lessons.title: What debt and equity cost
lessons.objective: Say why a firm's debt costs less than its equity, why that does not make borrowing cheap overall, and where each cost comes from.

concepts.title: Cost of debt
concepts.summary: What lenders require on new borrowing today: the risk-free rate plus a premium for the chance of default, less the value of the interest deduction.

concepts.title: Cost of equity
concepts.summary: What shareholders require: the risk-free rate plus a premium for the risk they carry; no contract promises it, but it is a cost all the same.

concepts.title: Priority of claims
concepts.summary: Lenders are paid before shareholders, who receive what is left, which may be nothing.

concepts.title: Leverage raises the cost of equity
concepts.summary: More debt leaves shareholders with a riskier residual, so they require more.

misconceptions: Equity is free because a company is not obliged to pay a dividend. Shareholders could earn a return elsewhere for the same risk, and that is the cost.
Debt is cheaper, so the more of it the better. More debt makes the equity riskier and lenders ask for more.
A firm's cost of debt is the coupon on its old bonds. It is what lenders require on new debt today.
Cost of debt equals the interest rate in the loan contract. It is the rate net of the tax value of the deduction and judged at market yield.
sequence: Open with a real failure: the CLEM7 tunnel, whose tolls did not cover interest on $1.3 billion of debt and whose shares became worthless.
Say why lenders and shareholders are paid in that order, and what it does to what each requires.
Build the cost of debt (risk-free plus default premium) and the cost of equity (risk-free plus market-risk premium).
Show Modigliani and Miller's second proposition in words: more debt raises the required return on equity.
Conclude that cheap debt does not make a cheap firm; the blend is the subject of lesson 8.
examples: Real: the Cross City Tunnel was funded with A$220 million of equity from three international companies and A$580 million from a syndicate of banks; in December 2006 it became insolvent and banks appointed receivers. The pack does not say what shareholders received.

lessons.title: WACC and hurdle rates
lessons.objective: Say what WACC measures, what raises or lowers it, and why a project should be judged at a rate that matches its own risk rather than the company's average.

concepts.title: Weighted average cost of capital
concepts.summary: The blend of what lenders and shareholders require, weighted by the market value of each and with interest taken after tax; set by the market, not by management.

concepts.title: Hurdle rate
concepts.summary: The return a project must beat; for a project like the rest of the firm it can be the WACC, otherwise it should match the project's own risk.

concepts.title: Project-specific rate
concepts.summary: A required return based on the systematic risk of the project, found from firms in the same line of business or by adjusting the WACC up or down.

concepts.title: WACC is an estimate
concepts.summary: Each input has several plausible proxies, so a fairly wide range of values can look defensible.

misconceptions: Management chooses the company's cost of capital. It is set by the external market.
One company rate fits every project. A safe project needs a lower rate than a cyclical one inside the same firm.
Adding cheap debt keeps lowering WACC. Past some point the cost of debt and equity both rise.
WACC is a precise number. Reasonable analysts reach quite different values for the same firm.

lessons.title: Why firms borrow

concepts.title: Financial leverage
concepts.summary: Borrowing to fund assets so that owners' return rises when the assets earn more than the debt costs, and falls further when they earn less.

concepts.title: Tax shield
concepts.summary: The tax saved because interest is deductible while dividends are not.

concepts.title: Modigliani-Miller without taxes
concepts.summary: In a perfect market with no taxes or distress costs, the mix of debt and equity does not change firm value.

concepts.title: Dividend imputation
concepts.summary: Company tax is passed to shareholders as a credit, so profit paid to eligible shareholders is taxed at their own rate.

misconceptions: Borrowing always raises the owners' return. It does only when the assets earn more than the debt costs, and it makes a bad year worse.
In theory debt creates value. With no taxes, Modigliani and Miller show it does not; it matters because of taxes and other frictions.
Interest and dividends are treated the same for tax. Interest is deductible; dividends are not.
A more indebted firm is always riskier. A utility with steady cash flows can be safer with debt than a technology firm without.

Bring in Australia: under imputation the company tax paid on distributed profit is credited to eligible shareholders; say what that does to the weight of company tax.

lessons.title: Distress and the trade-off
lessons.objective: Judge whether a firm should borrow more by weighing the tax benefit of debt against the costs of financial distress, given how steady its cash flows are.

concepts.title: Financial distress
concepts.summary: A condition in which promises to creditors are broken or honoured with difficulty; it has direct costs (fees) and indirect costs (higher interest, lost attention, lost projects).

concepts.title: Trade-off theory
concepts.summary: Firms balance the tax benefit of debt against the cost of bankruptcy and distress.

concepts.title: Interest cover
concepts.summary: Profit before interest divided by the interest bill: how many times the interest could be paid out of profit.

concepts.title: Debt overhang
concepts.summary: Existing debt so large that the firm cannot take on a good new investment because the gains would go to lenders.

concepts.title: Pecking order
concepts.summary: Firms prefer internal funds, then debt, and raise equity last, because outsiders read a share issue as bad news.

misconceptions: Distress only costs money in bankruptcy. Interest rates rise and management attention and good projects are lost before then.
The debt ratio alone says how risky a firm is. Volatility of cash flow matters as much.
A firm that can deduct interest should borrow as much as possible. Distress costs rise as debt rises.
Debt is a harmless way of funding projects. With heavy debt, shareholders may favour risky projects and refuse safe good ones.

lessons.title: Dividends, buybacks and franking credits
lessons.objective: Judge whether a firm should pay cash out or keep it, whether to use a dividend or a buyback, and what a franked dividend is worth to different shareholders.

concepts.title: Payout ratio
concepts.summary: Dividends as a share of earnings (or of free cash flow); above 100% means paying out more than was earned.

concepts.title: Residual dividend policy
concepts.summary: Invest in every project that beats the required return, then pay out what is left.

concepts.title: Share buyback
concepts.summary: The company buys its own shares; earnings per share rise because there are fewer shares.

concepts.title: Franking credit
concepts.summary: A credit for company tax already paid, passed on with a dividend; usable by eligible Australian taxpayers, refundable to some.

concepts.title: Signalling
concepts.summary: A rise in the dividend, or a buyback, may tell the market that management is confident or thinks the shares are cheap.

misconceptions: A dividend is a gift on top of the company's value. It moves value from the company to the owner; in a perfect market the share price falls by about the dividend.
A buyback creates value because earnings per share rise. They rise because there are fewer shares.
A payout above 100% is just generosity. It means paying out more than was earned, and needs cash from somewhere.
A franking credit is cash from the company. It is a tax credit usable only by eligible Australian taxpayers.
All Australian dividends are fully franked. Lovisa paid unfranked and part-franked dividends.
sequence: Start from the simplest question: a firm has surplus cash and a project that earns less than owners could earn elsewhere. Should it pay out?
Show the payout ratio and its caution, with Lovisa's five-year table where dividends exceeded profit in four years.
Say what the theory says (irrelevant in a perfect market; tax and signalling matter) and where buybacks differ.
Explain imputation using the ATO's worked example, and say who can use credits.
Read Woolworths (fully franked) against Lovisa (unfranked and 50% franked) as a contrast in what is passed on.
Close on what to ask of any payout: is it covered by cash, would the money earn more inside the firm, and who receives it?
examples: Invented: a firm has $50m of surplus cash; its best project earns 5% and owners could earn 9% on similar risk elsewhere. It should pay out. If the project earned 14%, it should keep the cash.

lessons.title: Forecasts and sensitivity
lessons.objective: Find which assumption a project's value hinges on, work out how far it can move before the answer flips, and judge a forecast against what happened to similar projects.

concepts.title: Sensitivity analysis
concepts.summary: Changing one input at a time to see how far the answer moves; it shows which forecasts deserve effort.

concepts.title: Break-even input
concepts.summary: The value of an assumption at which NPV is zero.

concepts.title: Scenario analysis
concepts.summary: Changing linked inputs together, such as price and volume.

concepts.title: Outside view (reference class forecasting)
concepts.summary: Forecasting from the outcomes of similar past projects instead of from the details of this one.

concepts.title: Planning fallacy
concepts.summary: The tendency to underestimate time, cost and risk and overestimate benefits.

misconceptions: The base case is the expected case. Forecasts of costs and benefits tend to be optimistic.
Varying every input by the same percentage shows which matters. What matters is how far each could plausibly be wrong.
One-at-a-time changes are enough. Price and volume move together, so they belong in a scenario.
A positive NPV at the base case means a safe project. It may turn on a single assumption.
sequence: Show a project with a positive NPV at its base case and ask what could go wrong.
Run one-at-a-time changes and read the table: price and volume matter far more than costs.
Find break-even values: how far price or volume can fall.
Show the real cases where one assumption decided everything: CLEM7 and the Cross City Tunnel.
Introduce the outside view, with the Sydney Opera House as an Australian example.
Read Woolworths' notes on New Zealand Food and Petstock as sensitivity analysis done in a real report.
examples: Invented project: outlay $2.0m; 8 years; 12,000 units at $100, variable cost $55 a unit, fixed cost $120,000 a year; 9% rate. NPV about +$325,000.

One at a time (NPV, $000): price -10%: -340; volume -20%: -273; variable cost +10%: -41; fixed cost +20%: +192; rate +2 points: +161; life 6 years: -116; outlay +20%: -75. Break-even: price about 5% lower ($95.1), volume about 11% lower (about 10,700 units). Price -10% together with volume -20%: about -805.

CLEM7: forecast about 60,000 trips a day; 59,000 a day with no toll but about 20,000 with the reduced toll; forecast ramp-up to 100,000 a day in 2012, with no ramp-up by March 2011. Cross City Tunnel: expected about 35,000 a day at first, rising to 90,000; about 20,000 reported a month after opening against 25,000 claimed by government and operators. Sydney Opera House: expected 1963, opened 1973; $7 million estimate, $102 million cost.

Woolworths: New Zealand Food needs only a 1.0 point rise in rate and a 10% cut in terminal-year EBIT to lose its headroom; Petstock needs 0.2 points and 4%, and 'relies on continued growth and synergies' after a recent acquisition.

lessons.title: Acquisitions and the price paid
lessons.objective: Judge whether an acquisition price can pay off by comparing the premium with the synergies the buyer can realistically deliver, and say how competition and overconfidence push buyers to overpay.

concepts.title: Control premium
concepts.summary: The amount a buyer pays over the market price to gain control of a listed company.

concepts.title: Synergy
concepts.summary: A benefit a buyer expects from combining the businesses; cost synergies are trusted more than revenue synergies.

concepts.title: Winner's curse
concepts.summary: In a contest where all bidders value the prize about the same, the winner is the one with the most optimistic estimate, and so tends to overpay.

concepts.title: Managerial overconfidence
concepts.summary: Managers overrate the synergies, and so overpay.

misconceptions: The synergies belong to the buyer. A large premium hands them to the seller's shareholders.
Combining businesses creates value by itself. Diversifying gives shareholders nothing they could not do in their own portfolios.
Winning a competitive bid shows a good deal. Winning is bad news about the value of the prize.
A high price proves an overpayment. The price must be compared with the cash flows the business later delivers.
sequence: Show a bid: market value, premium, and the synergies the buyer claims.
Compare the premium with the synergies, and ask who captures the gain.
Cut the synergies that are delivered and see where the buyer's gain disappears.
Add the pack's warnings: motives that do not add value, and revenue synergies that often fail to appear.
Show the winner's curse in a five-bidder contest.
Read three real cases: Rio Tinto and Riversdale, Rio Tinto and Alcan, and Woolworths' thin headroom on Petstock and its full write-downs.
examples: Invented: a target with a market value of $1,000m; the buyer thinks the combination is worth $120m more. A 35% premium is $350m: even if all the synergies arrive the buyer loses $230m; if half arrive, $290m. A 10% premium is $100m: the buyer gains $20m if all arrive and loses $64m if only 30% do.
Invented winner's curse: five bidders estimate a block worth $100m at $70m, $85m, $100m, $115m and $130m. The $130m bidder wins and pays far more than the block is worth.

Rio Tinto bought the Australian coal miner Riversdale for $2.9 billion in cash, wrote the assets down by $3 billion two years later, and later sold them for $50 million. Rio Tinto bought Alcan for US$38 billion in 2007, a deal that undermined a hostile US$27.5 billion bid from Alcoa; the pack says nothing about the result.

Woolworths: the valuation of Petstock 'relies on continued growth and synergies with the Group', and the carrying values of the BIG W, MyDeal and Healthylife units were fully impaired in the prior period.

lessons.title: What a share price tells you
lessons.objective: Judge from a piece of news whether a share price should move, say what the efficient-market idea does and does not claim, and decide what a manager can and cannot read from the market's price.

concepts.title: Efficient-market hypothesis
concepts.summary: Prices reflect all available information, so prices move only on new information and nobody can consistently beat the market on a risk-adjusted basis.

concepts.title: Surprise
concepts.summary: Only the part of news that differs from what was expected moves the price.

concepts.title: Weak, semi-strong and strong forms
concepts.summary: The information in question is past prices, all public information, or private information as well.

concepts.title: Event study
concepts.summary: Reading the effect of an event on a firm's value from its share price around the event.

misconceptions: Good news raises the price. Only news better than expected does.
Efficient markets mean prices are always right, or never fall. They mean prices reflect available information, and new information can lower them.
Efficiency means analysis is pointless. Prices reflect the work of the people who analyse.
A bid above the market price shows the market was wrong. A control premium pays for control and expected gains.
The evidence settles it. The sources say it is mixed and disputed.
sequence: Open on Lovisa's table: earnings per share rose in 2026 while the share price fell.
State the efficient-market idea and its mechanism: traders act on information until it is gone.
Read news against expectations in a set of announcements.
Use CLEM7: a share price that dropped by a fifth on traffic figures and later fell to nothing.
Show the three forms and the disputes about them, so the claim is held at its true strength.
Say what managers can do with the price: read it as information, notice that a control premium is a price for control, and remember that a buyback may be a bet on undervaluation.
examples: Lovisa, 2022 to 2026: earnings per share 54.3, 63.3, 75.4, 78.1, 86.3 cents; share price $14.26, $19.30, $32.87, $30.91, $23.25. In 2026 earnings per share rose 10.5% and the price fell by about a quarter.

Invented: analysts expect profit to rise 5%. Reported rises of 5%, 9% and 1%: price unchanged, up, down.
